A chapter-by-chapter reading of the Daodejing, starting at the beginning. Chapter 1 is not an introduction to the Dao. It is a chapter about the sentence you are reading.

## The chapter

> 道可道，非常道；名可名，非常名。  
> 无，名天地之始；有，名万物之母。  
> 故常「无」，欲以观其妙；常「有」，欲以观其徼。  
> 此两者，同出而异名，同谓之玄。玄之又玄，众妙之门。

A literal rendering:

> The way that can be spoken is not the constant way; the name that can be named is not the constant name.  
> "Wu" — this names the beginning of heaven and earth; "you" — this names the mother of the ten thousand things.  
> Therefore, hold "wu" constantly, and with that intent look at its 妙; hold "you" constantly, and with that intent look at its 徼.  
> These two emerge together but have different names; together they are called 玄. Dark and darker — the gate of all that is subtle.

Four lines, four moves, fifty-nine characters. Everything else in the book is downstream.

## Move one: the limit of the tool

The first line does not say the Dao is ineffable. It says something more precise: whatever you manage to say is already not the constant thing. The problem is not speech as such; it is that a spoken 道 is a made 道 — which is why the same sentence immediately repeats the move for names.

This is the chapter's self-referential move. It is using names to mark the limit of naming, and it does so at the first opportunity, before any doctrine is offered. A text that begins this way is telling you how to hold everything that follows: as a finger pointing, not as the thing pointed at.

The usual paraphrase — "the Tao that can be told is not the eternal Tao" — is close, but it flattens the second clause, where 名 does the real work. 名 is not just a label. In pre-Qin usage, naming is the act that installs a boundary: 名不正则言不顺, said Confucius, meaning that if the names are wrong the sentences won't hold. To name is to place something in a system of distinctions. The chapter's first move is to say: this system is useful, and it is not the world.

## Move two: two names, not two things

Then 无 and 有 enter — and the way they enter matters. They are introduced as names: 无，名天地之始. Not "nothingness is the beginning," but "'wu' names the beginning."

Read that way, the line is not a cosmogony. It is a statement about two positions inside the naming system:

- 无 marks what has not yet divided — no boundary, no contour, no name applied. Not "empty space," but the unmarked state before distinctions.
- 有 marks what has already divided — contour, boundary, the ten thousand things as distinguishable.

The chapter then does something odd and precise: it tells you to hold each of them 常 — constantly — and look. Not to prefer one, not to pass from one to the other, but to use each as a fixed frame and see what it shows.

- Under 无, you see 妙: written 玅 in older forms, 玄 plus 少 — the barely-there, the part that has not resolved into shape, the small opening through which something can still emerge.
- Under 有, you see 徼, read jiào: the boundary that lights up once life has unfolded. Not a wall, but the natural contour that appears when a thing takes its measure.

Same object, two frames. This is the point that most translations lose by turning 无 and 有 into nouns of substance, and then arguing about whether the universe began in nothing.

## Move three: 玄 is not "mystery"

此两者，同出而异名，同谓之玄.

玄 is usually translated "mystery" or "darkness." The character is two threads twisted together — the image is inseparability, not obscurity. Two names, one source; you cannot separate them without losing both. The wall and the hollow of a cup: take one away and the other is not there either.

玄之又玄 is not "mystery upon mystery," a recommendation to stop thinking. It is the twist doubled: the two frames are themselves not two, and that not-two is also not a third thing. Each attempt to say it adds another layer that has to be marked as a layer. The line is a description of what happens when you keep trying to say it accurately.

## Move four: the gate is a hinge

众妙之门. 门 in pre-Qin usage is not only a doorway; it is the hinge point where opening and closing happen — the place where a thing can pass from unmarked to marked.

So the chapter ends not with a destination but with a mechanism. The gate of all subtle things is the point where 无 and 有 turn into each other, where a name is applied and a contour appears, where a contour dissolves and the position opens again. It is not somewhere you go. It is the place you are already standing, every time you name something.

## What this does to a reader

The practical instruction is small and testable: for one day, notice every place where you treat a name as a thing.

Not as an exercise in doubt — the name still works, the cup still holds water — but as a way of seeing that the name arrived with a boundary attached, and that the boundary was chosen, often by someone else, often for reasons that no longer hold.

That is what the rest of the book does with 无为, with 柔弱, with 不争. None of it is mysticism. It is applied attention to where the boundary was drawn.

## Textual notes

- 常 vs 恒: the Wang Bi received text has 常; the Mawangdui silk manuscripts have 恒 (constant, enduring). The difference is small but real, and this edition keeps both.
- The 也 at the end of the Mawangdui lines is not the syntactic veto it is often claimed to be. I wrote about that separately, because arguments about punctuation tend to substitute for arguments about meaning.
- Punctuation: this edition reads 常「无」，欲以观其妙; 常「有」，欲以观其徼 — not 常无欲 / 常有欲. 欲 here is intent, the direction attention is set, not appetite.
